lab.name: Geotechnical Earthquake and GeoHazards Lab
lab.intro: GEHL studies how earthquakes and related geohazards affect soils, foundations, and the infrastructure built on them. We combine geotechnical centrifuge modeling, numerical simulation, analytical methods, probabilistic uncertainty quantification, and earthquake case histories to evaluate what has happened, predict what could happen, and design urban systems that stay resilient through natural disasters.

core.title: A reliable, realistic, and interactive seismic risk map
paragraphs: GEHL's vision is a seismic risk map that is reliable, realistic, and interactive: one that engineers, planners, and the public can trust and use. Every project in the lab is a step toward it, and every project follows one chain: characterize the input motion, identify the soil-foundation-structure system, and predict its output. The same framework is being extended from earthquakes to other natural hazards.

Reaching that map takes methods at every scale, from the laboratory to the city. Laboratory and centrifuge tests expose the micro-mechanics of soil at the particle scale; centrifuge and numerical modeling capture the response of single and multiple structures as one system; and site characterization, from shear-wave velocity profiles to earthquake case histories and drone-based surveys, builds the liquefaction hazard and ground-motion models behind the map. Experimental, numerical, and analytical results are checked against recorded earthquakes from databases such as DesignSafe, KiK-net, and CESMD, and probabilistic methods carry the uncertainty through to the final risk estimate.

framework.s: Ground-motion characterization, seismic source and fault modeling, site response
Soil, foundation, and structure as one dynamic system: centrifuge tests, element tests, numerical models
Settlement, rotation, pore pressure, cracking, and erosion, with their uncertainty

core.loop: Validated against earthquake case histories and fed back into design
core.figureCaption: Methods for GEHL's vision, from laboratory to urban scale: laboratory tests and centrifuge modeling for micro-mechanics, centrifuge and numerical modeling for system-level response, and site characterization for seismic hazard and risk maps.

areas.title: Dynamic Soil-Foundation-Structure Interaction
paragraphs: Seismic design usually treats the structure and the ground separately. We measure how they move together, so that the interaction can be used in design rather than ignored. Dynamic centrifuge tests on shallow foundations, rocking foundations, and disconnected piled rafts give the data; analytical models that couple horizontal structural response with foundation rocking and swaying turn the data into predictions.

Rocking shallow foundations are a good example: rocking reduces the demand on the superstructure but leaves permanent deformation, so the question is how to use it safely. Short piles, the soil-rounding effect, cyclic versus dynamic rocking, and ground-motion intensity measures for rocking performance all come from this line of work.
topics: Rocking shallow foundations and short piles

areas.title: Energy-Based Soil Liquefaction Assessment
paragraphs: We use the energy dissipated in the soil, rather than cyclic stress alone, to estimate the buildup of excess pore pressure. This makes it possible to evaluate liquefaction without pore-water-pressure transducers, to read the timing of liquefaction directly from recorded ground motions through the spectral energy ratio, and to treat dissipated energy as an index of liquefiability.

The framework has been validated against case histories such as the 2003 Tokachi-Oki earthquake at the Port of Kushiro and the 2017 Pohang earthquake, and extended into a probabilistic energy-based framework that connects triggering to consequences such as settlement. Ongoing work builds a multi-scale framework for integrated cyclic loadings and a probabilistic liquefaction hazard assessment for the Pohang region.
topics: Spectral energy ratio and timing of liquefaction
Depth reduction factor in liquefiable layers

areas.title: Cracking and Concentrated Leak Erosion due to Fault Rupture
paragraphs: Many embankment dams sit on or near active faults. A vertical offset in the foundation can crack the crest, and water flowing through that crack can erode the core. We estimate crack dimensions from the offset and judge the erosion potential from the erodibility and swelling of the core material.

Triaxial, swell, erosion, and beam-bending tests characterize the soil; centrifuge tests with controlled foundation offsets, run in collaboration with UC Davis, Auburn University, and the California Department of Water Resources, show how cracks propagate and how fast water moves through them; numerical models carry the mechanism to prototype scale.
topics: Scaling of flow through transverse cracks
Risk assessment with the RMC toolbox

areas.eyebrow: Research area 4 | Site response and ground motion
areas.title: Seismic Site Response, Topographic Effects, and Ground Motion
paragraphs: The motion that reaches a foundation depends on the source, the path, and the site. We work on seismic source and fault modeling, ground-motion characterization for Korean and global conditions, and one- and two-dimensional site response analysis, including the amplification caused by topography.

Dynamic centrifuge tests of slopes and ridges quantify topographic effect parameters on site amplification, and geophysical investigation (for example MASW) ties the models to real sites. The results feed national seismic design scenarios for mountainous terrain.

interests: Seismic source characterization and fault modeling
Dynamic soil-structure interaction (SSI) and structure-soil-structure interaction (SSSI)
Fault-rupture-induced cracking and crack propagation in earthen dams and levees
Physical modeling in geotechnics: centrifuge modeling and scaling laws

courses.title: Introduction to Geotechnical Engineering
courses.text: Geotechnical terminology and the fundamentals of soil mechanics: phase relationships, classification, compaction, effective stress, fluid flow, consolidation and settlement, and shear strength. Laboratory classes are included. The course prepares students for foundation engineering, dam engineering, soil dynamics, and geotechnical earthquake engineering.

courses.title: Advanced Soil Dynamics
courses.text: Dynamics of simple systems (waves, vibrations, single-degree-of-freedom systems), dynamic soil properties (G/Gmax and damping versus strain), waves in infinite and bounded media, and one-dimensional site response analysis. The course gives the theoretical foundation for geotechnical earthquake engineering.

courses.title: Advanced Geomechanics
courses.text: Stress- and state-dependent behavior of sands and clays: dilatancy, drained and undrained strength, and stress paths. Critical state soil mechanics and simple models (Mohr–Coulomb, Cam-clay) are used to interpret laboratory tests and to analyze soil strength and deformation.

teachingPhilosophy: New research and new technology keep expanding what is known, so a teacher has to keep learning and recognize quickly which new developments matter. That takes a firm grip on the fundamentals. The aim in every course is to close the gap between established and new research, to connect fundamental theory with practice, and to help students become self-directed engineers who can solve problems that did not exist when they were students.

culture.lead: Research begins where something does not work. We go after unsolved problems and trace them back to fundamentals, with the freedom of structured autonomy: flexible but clear guidelines, self-directed growth, and teamwork.

lookingFor.title: Teamwork
lookingFor.text: We share data, code, failures, and credit. Progress in a centrifuge lab is a team result.

lookingFor.title: A mechanics-oriented mindset
lookingFor.text: Tools change; equilibrium, compatibility, and constitutive behavior do not. We want people who reason from mechanics first.

lookingFor.title: Logical communication
lookingFor.text: A clear argument, in a figure or a paragraph, is as much a research skill as a good test.

lookingFor.title: Persistence and resilience
lookingFor.text: Tests fail, models diverge, and reviewers push back. Keep going, and learn from what broke.

lookingFor.title: Clear storytelling
lookingFor.text: Research has to be explained to colleagues, practitioners, and the public.

lookingFor.title: Self-motivation
lookingFor.text: Curiosity and a sense of engineering responsibility carry a project further than any schedule.

culture.positions: We welcome undergraduate interns and graduate students (M.S. and Ph.D.) who are interested in geotechnical earthquake engineering and natural hazards. Character and mindset matter as much as academic record: an inquisitive spirit, persistence, respect, humility, and logical thinking. We are always open to discussing methodologies, research ideas, and emerging topics.

teaching.goal: World-best decision makers and leaders in risk assessment
teaching.lead: Courses at GEHL are built on the experiential learning cycle and use every sense a student has. Each class moves from feeling to talking to thinking to doing: a concrete experience, reflection and discussion on it, a concept that explains it, and an experiment that tests it. The aim is engineers who can make decisions about seismic risk, not only calculate it.

cycle.d: Centrifuge tests, laboratory experiments, and earthquake damage are the starting point. Homework asks students to run an experiment or study a case history before the theory is introduced.
Case histories from past earthquakes are introduced and discussed in class, so that students put what they saw into words and compare interpretations.
Recorded motions, site response, and the mechanics behind them turn the observation into a concept the student can carry to a new problem.
Students test the concept in new experiments, analyses, and designs, which produces the next concrete experience and closes the loop.

teaching.figureCaption: Teaching philosophy at GEHL: the experiential learning cycle (concrete experience, observation and reflection, abstract conceptualization, active experimentation) run with experiments, case histories, and recorded ground motions.
teaching.quote: Learning through Experience, Growing through Discussion, and Opening the future through Innovation
